summary: This document requires that TLS clients and servers never negotiate the use of RC4 cipher suites, for all TLS versions. It updates RFC 5246, RFC 4346, and RFC 2246.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7465 prohibits TLS clients and servers from negotiating cipher suites that use RC4. It applies to all TLS versions and makes a handshake fail if the client offers only RC4 suites.

questions: why was rc4 banned in tls
what happens if a client only offers rc4
which tls versions does rfc 7465 update
subtitle: Prohibit TLS clients and servers from negotiating RC4 cipher suites.

tldr.problem: RC4 has cryptographic weaknesses, including biases that can help recover plaintext encrypted repeatedly with the cipher.
tldr.mechanism: Clients MUST NOT offer RC4 cipher suites, and servers MUST NOT select them. A server MUST end a handshake if the client offers only RC4 suites.
tldr.outcome: RC4 suites cannot be negotiated in the TLS versions covered by RFC 7465. The RFC updates RFC 2246, RFC 4346, and RFC 5246 and is updated by RFC 8996.

facts.label: ClientHello rule
facts.value: Must not include RC4 cipher suites

today: RFC 7465 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2015. It updates RFC 2246, RFC 4346, and RFC 5246; the unit metadata says RFC 8996 updates it.

sections.title: Why RC4 Is Prohibited
sections.content:
RC4 is a stream cipher that was widely supported by TLS servers. The RFC notes that cryptographic weaknesses had been known for some time.

More recent analysis exploited biases in the RC4 keystream to recover plaintexts encrypted repeatedly. The RFC says the attacks then required 2^26 sessions or 13x2^30 encryptions, and concludes RC4 no longer provides sufficient security for TLS.
sections.plainLanguage: Research found weaknesses in RC4 that could expose text encrypted with it many times. The RFC therefore prohibits using RC4 to protect TLS sessions.

sections.title: The Three TLS Requirements
sections.content:
The rules apply to all TLS versions named in the RFC. A TLS client MUST NOT include RC4 cipher suites in its ClientHello.

A TLS server MUST NOT select an RC4 suite, even if the client includes one. If the client offers only RC4 suites, the server MUST terminate the handshake and MAY send the fatal insufficient_security alert.
sections.plainLanguage: A client cannot request RC4, and a server cannot choose it. If RC4 is the client's only offer, the server ends the connection setup.

sections.title: What Happens During the Handshake
sections.content:
During a TLS handshake, the client lists supported cipher suites in ClientHello, and the server selects one of them. This RFC removes RC4 suites from the acceptable choices.

If the server cannot select an allowed suite, it does not fall back to RC4. It terminates the handshake, so the connection is not established with that cipher.
sections.plainLanguage: The server chooses from the suites offered by the client, but it must ignore any RC4 suite. A handshake ends if there is no other acceptable choice.

sections.title: The RC4 Suites Covered
sections.content:
Appendix A lists the TLS cipher suites that use RC4. The list includes RSA, anonymous Diffie-Hellman, Kerberos, pre-shared key, and elliptic-curve suite families.

Examples include TLS_RSA_WITH_RC4_128_SHA, TLS_RSA_WITH_RC4_128_MD5, and TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_RC4_128_SHA. Export suites with a 40-bit key are included as well.
sections.plainLanguage: The appendix names the RC4 suites explicitly, including suites from several key-exchange families. A TLS implementation can use this list to identify the prohibited choices.

sections.title: Maintaining TLS Security
sections.content:
The security consideration is direct: prohibiting RC4-based cipher suites helps maintain the security guarantees of TLS. The RFC states that those suites do not provide a sufficiently high level of security.

The prohibition is achieved through the client and server requirements in Section 2, including terminating the handshake when the client offers only RC4 suites.
sections.plainLanguage: The prohibition keeps TLS from using cipher suites the RFC considers too weak. A connection must fail rather than negotiate RC4 as a fallback.
